body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Nurse-led telephone review during the percutaneous trial of spinal cord stimulation: a before-after service evaluation","authors":"Aldridge-Mensah P, Kowalczyk-Reid T, Obi-Lindqvist H","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Neuromodulation Nursing","doi":"10.5555/jnn.2021.0317","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Background: patients having a percutaneous spinal cord stimulation trial usually attend clinic during the trial week. Methods: one regional service replaced the mid-trial clinic visit with a structured nurse telephone review and compared 102 trials in the year before the change with 97 trials in the year after. Results: unplanned attendances during the trial week were 11 of 102 before and 12 of 97 after. The proportion of patients reaching a permanent implant decision on the planned day was 89 percent before and 91 percent after. Median nurse time per telephone review was 18 minutes. Conclusions: replacing the mid-trial visit with a telephone review was not followed by more unplanned attendances in this service. Costs were not measured."},{"title":"Costs to patients of attending neuromodulation clinics: travel, time off work and companions","authors":"Brennan-Oduya S, Haverkamp-Li J","year":2018,"venue":"Pain Services Research Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We asked 214 consecutive patients attending a regional neuromodulation clinic to complete a short questionnaire about the cost of the visit. The median round trip was 96 km and the median time away from home was five and a half hours. Most patients (58 percent) were accompanied by a relative or friend, and the companion lost a working day in 41 percent of visits. The median out-of-pocket cost per visit, including fuel, parking and meals, was 34 in local currency. Patients living in rural postcodes reported the highest costs, and several said they had delayed reporting problems to avoid an extra trip."},{"title":"Infection after percutaneous spinal cord stimulation trials: timing and presentation in 1,140 trials","authors":"Castellano-Fry M, Nwachukwu-Berg A, Tamsin-Oyelaran R","year":2020,"venue":"Regional Anaesthesia and Pain Outcomes","doi":"10.5555/rapo.2020.0088","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed the records of 1,140 percutaneous spinal cord stimulation trials performed at five centres to describe when trial-related infections appear and how they are found. Infection occurred in 27 trials (2.4 percent). Of the 27 infections, 21 were first noticed after day 5 of the trial and 19 were first reported by the patient rather than found at a scheduled visit. Wound discharge and new pain at the exit site were the usual first signs. No centre found an infection at a scheduled day 3 visit that the patient had not already reported. Diabetes and a trial longer than ten days were associated with infection."},{"title":"Telephone versus face-to-face follow-up after interventional pain procedures: a randomised non-inferiority trial","authors":"Delacroix-Amadi N, Fenwick-Soto L","year":2016,"venue":"Clinical Pain Pathways","doi":"10.5555/cpp.2016.0412","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"We randomised 240 adults who had radiofrequency denervation or a spinal cord stimulator implant to telephone or face-to-face follow-up two weeks after the procedure. The primary outcome was satisfaction with follow-up on a 10-point scale. Mean satisfaction was 8.6 with telephone and 8.8 with face-to-face follow-up, within the non-inferiority margin. Unplanned visits in the following month occurred in 7 percent of the telephone group and 6 percent of the face-to-face group. Telephone calls took a median of 12 minutes of clinician time against 25 minutes per clinic appointment. Patients with hearing impairment or who needed an interpreter were excluded."},{"title":"Remote follow-up in neuromodulation and interventional pain care: a systematic review","authors":"Ferreira-Nakamura C, Oyelowo-Brandt E, Lindgren-Achebe K","year":2023,"venue":"Pain Medicine Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/pmer.2023.0140","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We searched four bibliographic databases to December 2022 for studies comparing remote and in-person follow-up after neuromodulation or interventional pain procedures. Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria: two randomised trials and 11 observational comparisons. Remote follow-up reduced patient travel in every study that measured it, and unplanned attendances were similar where reported. Safety outcomes such as infection were rarely defined in advance. Two studies reported costs to the health service, neither with an analysis of uncertainty. No study included an economic evaluation from the patient perspective. Most studies were at serious risk of bias from historical comparison groups."},{"title":"Unit costs of outpatient pain clinic activity: a micro-costing study","authors":"Grayson-Mbeki O, Iwasaki-Holt D","year":2022,"venue":"Health Service Costing Notes","providerType":"report","abstract":"We observed 312 outpatient pain clinic contacts with time-and-motion methods and combined staff time with salary, overhead and room costs to estimate a cost per contact. A nurse-led telephone review cost 21 per contact, a nurse clinic appointment 64 and a consultant appointment 148 at 2021 prices. Overheads made up 38 percent of the cost of a clinic appointment. A telephone contact that led to a same-day clinic review cost the sum of both contacts. The estimates came from one hospital and exclude patient and companion costs."},{"title":"Aftercare during spinal cord stimulation trials: a consensus statement from a national neuromodulation nursing forum","authors":"National Neuromodulation Nursing Forum","year":2025,"venue":"Neuromodulation Practice Guidance","doi":"10.5555/npg.2025.0003","providerType":"guideline","abstract":"A panel of 14 neuromodulation nurses and physicians reached consensus on aftercare during the trial of spinal cord stimulation using two rounds of structured voting. The panel recommends that every patient has a named contact for the trial week, a wound check by day 3 either in person or by a structured remote review, and an in-person review before lead removal. The panel found no comparative evidence on the timing of wound checks and did not consider costs. Recommendations on remote review assume that the patient can use a telephone and describe the wound."}]}
